scope: Selected major periods of political control; names that disclose the answer are generalized. Notes and linked sources explain local scope, approximation and omitted interruptions.

cities.name: Salzburg

periods.label: Austria
periods.detail: Austria: republic, then authoritarian federal state

periods.label: Austria (US occupation)
periods.detail: Restored Austria under US occupation

cities.note: The 1805 treaty transferred Salzburg to Austria; Austrian administration began in 1806. Bavaria ruled from 1810, not 1809. Austria-Hungary began in 1867. German-Austria lasted only 1918–1919; the authoritarian Federal State of Austria was 1934–1938. Brief Napoleonic occupations in 1800 and 1805 are omitted.

sources.title: Salzburg Museum — five changes of ruler
City of Salzburg — Austrian and Bavarian administration

cities.name: Vienna

periods.label: Austria
periods.detail: Austria: republic, then authoritarian federal state

periods.label: Austria (Allied occupation)
periods.detail: Restored Austria under four-power Allied occupation

cities.note: This timeline begins with the Austrian Empire. Vienna had already been a Habsburg seat within the Holy Roman Empire. French occupations in 1805 and 1809 were brief. After 1945 the city was divided among Soviet, American, British and French sectors, with a jointly administered centre.

cities.name: Prague

periods.label: Nazi Germany
periods.detail: German occupation: Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia

cities.note: The Habsburg period is a broad dynastic summary: the 1618–1620 Bohemian revolt and brief military occupations are not separate rows. Czechoslovakia included democratic and communist governments; Soviet-led forces invaded in 1968, without annexing the city.

cities.name: Budapest

periods.label: Hungary (Austrian rule)
periods.detail: Kingdom of Hungary (Austrian emperors)

periods.detail: Hungary under Soviet occupation and increasing communist control

cities.note: Before the 1873 union of Buda, Pest and Óbuda, this timeline follows Buda. The 1918–1920 row groups the democratic republic, Soviet republic, Romanian occupation and transition to the restored monarchy. Soviet troops captured Budapest in February 1945.

sources.title: Buda in the medieval Kingdom of Hungary and Ottoman Empire

cities.name: Bratislava

periods.label: Hungary (Austrian rule)
periods.detail: Kingdom of Hungary (Austrian emperors)

periods.label: Slovakia (German client state)
periods.detail: Slovak Republic (German client state; occupied from 1944)

cities.note: The city became the capital of Habsburg Hungary in 1536. Czechoslovak troops secured the historic centre in January 1919. This follows that centre: Petržalka and Devín, now boroughs, were separately annexed by Germany in 1938.

cities.name: Ljubljana

periods.label: Habsburg Carniola (Holy Roman Empire)
periods.detail: Habsburg Carniola within the Holy Roman Empire

periods.label: Yugoslavia
periods.detail: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes / Yugoslavia

cities.note: The French interlude ended with Austrian recovery in 1813, before the international settlement. The short-lived State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs preceded the kingdom in late 1918. Italy annexed Ljubljana in 1941; German control followed Italy’s 1943 surrender.

cities.name: Trieste

periods.label: Habsburg Austria (Holy Roman Empire)
periods.detail: Habsburg Austria within the Holy Roman Empire

periods.label: Free territory (Allied administration)
periods.detail: Free territory, Zone A under Anglo-American administration

cities.note: Trieste submitted to Habsburg protection in 1382. French occupation briefly interrupted that relationship in 1797 and 1805. Italian troops arrived in 1918; treaty recognition followed in 1920. Italy took civil administration in 1954; the final border agreement was signed in 1975.

cities.name: Gorizia

periods.label: Italy
periods.detail: Italy (occupation, then annexation)

periods.label: Nazi Germany
periods.detail: Nazi German occupation: Adriatic Littoral

periods.label: Yugoslav / Allied occupation
periods.detail: Yugoslav occupation, then Allied military administration

cities.note: The timeline follows the historic town, not Nova Gorica. Gorizia had belonged to the Habsburgs since 1500 before the French interlude. Italian troops took it in August 1916; Austria-Hungary recovered it after Caporetto. The 1947 border left the old centre in Italy and several suburbs in Yugoslavia.

cities.name: Dubrovnik

periods.label: France

Austrians entered in 1814. Yugoslav Partisans took the city in October 1944. The 1991–1992 siege did not mean conquest of the old town.

cities.note: This follows control on the ground: Austrian forces returned in November 1813, with formal cession in 1815. The Napoleonic period is grouped under French control. Partisans briefly held Split after Italy surrendered in September 1943, before German occupation; lasting liberation came in 1944.

cities.name: Zadar

periods.label: Habsburg Austria
periods.detail: Habsburg monarchy, then Austrian Empire

periods.label: Napoleonic Italy

cities.note: Italy occupied Zadar in November 1918, with annexation recognized by the 1920 Treaty of Rapallo. Partisans took control in 1944; Italian sovereignty formally ended in 1947. The 1805 treaty transfer to Napoleonic Italy was implemented in 1806.

cities.name: Sarajevo

periods.label: Austro-Hungarian occupation under nominal Ottoman sovereignty
Austria-Hungary

periods.detail: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes / Yugoslavia

periods.detail: Independent State of Croatia (Axis puppet state)

cities.note: 1461 is the conventional founding date of Ottoman Sarajevo. Austro-Hungarian administration began in 1878, but formal annexation came only in 1908. The wartime city was besieged from 1992 to 1996; control around its edges was divided, so the final row follows the central city.

cities.name: Belgrade

periods.label: Ottoman Empire (Serbian autonomy)
periods.detail: Ottoman Empire, with growing Serbian autonomy after 1815

periods.label: Serbia
periods.detail: Independent Serbia (principality, then kingdom)

periods.label: Austro-Hungarian occupation

periods.detail: German military occupation with Serbian collaborationist administration

periods.label: Yugoslavia
periods.detail: Yugoslav Partisans, then socialist Yugoslavia

cities.note: This follows historic Belgrade, not formerly Habsburg Zemun across the river. Ottoman troops kept the fortress until 1867 despite Serbian civil autonomy. A brief Austro-Hungarian occupation in December 1914 is omitted. The kingdom was called the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes until 1929.

cities.name: Sofia

periods.label: Kingdom of Bulgaria
periods.detail: Kingdom of Bulgaria (Soviet occupation from 1944)

cities.note: The Ottoman conquest is variously dated 1382, 1383 or 1385. Russian troops took Sofia in January 1878; temporary Russian administration preceded the new principality. Bulgaria became fully independent in 1908. Soviet occupation in 1944 did not annex the city.

cities.name: Thessaloniki
cities.note: After an earlier Ottoman conquest, the city was returned to the Byzantines in 1403, handed to Venice in 1423 and conquered by the Ottomans in 1430. Greek troops entered in 1912; international recognition followed in 1913. Allied military presence and the rival Greek government during World War I are grouped under Greece.

cities.name: Athens

periods.label: Ottoman Empire
periods.detail: Ottoman Empire (Acropolis held by Greeks until 1827)

periods.label: Axis occupation
periods.detail: Axis occupation and collaborationist Hellenic State

cities.note: The Ottoman return began in the lower town in 1826; the Acropolis surrendered in 1827. Ottoman troops finally left in March 1833, after recognition of Greek independence. Greece here includes its successive monarchies, republics and military dictatorship.

cities.name: Istanbul

periods.label: Allied occupation
periods.detail: Allied occupation (Ottoman government until 1922)

cities.note: This timeline begins with Constantine’s refoundation as Constantinople in 330. Allied forces occupied the city after World War I, while the Ottoman sultanate continued until 1922. Turkish forces entered in October 1923, shortly before the republic was declared.

cities.name: Bucharest

periods.label: United Romanian principalities under Ottoman suzerainty
Central Powers occupation
periods.detail: German-led Central Powers occupation

periods.label: Kingdom of Romania
periods.detail: Kingdom of Romania (Soviet occupation from 1944)

cities.note: Wallachia and Moldavia shared a ruler from 1859 and formally united in 1862, when Bucharest became the capital. Independence was declared in 1877 and internationally recognized in 1878. German occupation lasted December 1916–November 1918. Soviet troops entered in 1944; the monarchy ended in 1947.

cities.name: Cluj-Napoca

periods.label: Kingdom of Hungary
periods.detail: Kingdom of Hungary (German occupation from March 1944)

periods.label: Soviet administration
periods.detail: Soviet military administration after joint Soviet-Romanian capture

cities.note: Habsburg military control preceded the 1699 treaty used here. Romanian forces entered in 1918, with sovereignty confirmed in 1920. Hungary regained the city through the 1940 Second Vienna Award. Soviet-Romanian troops captured it in October 1944; Romanian administration resumed in March 1945, with treaty confirmation in 1947.

sources.title: Cluj County Library — capture in October 1944

cities.name: Timișoara

periods.label: Habsburg crown province of the Banat
Austrian Empire
periods.detail: Austrian Empire (changing Hungarian and imperial provincial administration)

periods.label: Serbian occupation
periods.detail: Serbian military occupation after a short-lived regional republic

cities.note: Ottoman rule ended with the siege of 1716; treaty confirmation followed in 1718. Imperial authorities governed the Banat separately until 1779. The Banat Republic lasted briefly in November 1918 before Serbian occupation. Romanian troops entered in August 1919; the 1920 Treaty of Trianon formalized the transfer.

cities.name: Strasbourg

periods.label: Nazi Germany
periods.detail: Nazi German occupation and de facto annexation

cities.note: Strasbourg won independence from its bishop in 1262 and was seized by Louis XIV in 1681. This abridgement combines French constitutional regimes; German military capture in 1870 preceded the formal 1871 annexation. Liberation came in November 1944.

cities.name: Metz

periods.label: France (disputed sovereignty)
periods.detail: French royal control; imperial sovereignty disputed

periods.label: Nazi Germany
periods.detail: Nazi German occupation and de facto annexation

cities.note: The republic followed the citizens’ revolt against episcopal power in 1234. French possession from 1552 was internationally confirmed in 1648. French constitutional changes and the months between military capture and treaties are condensed.

cities.name: Nice
cities.note: The Savoyard period includes county and duchy status; short French occupations before 1792 and the Franco-Spanish occupation of 1744–1748 are omitted. Nice was ceded to France in 1860. Italian and German wartime occupations did not create lawful sovereignty.

cities.name: Perpignan

periods.label: Aragon / Spain
periods.detail: Crown of Aragon; later the Spanish monarchy

cities.note: Perpignan is documented from 927. French capture in 1642 preceded formal cession by Spain in 1659. These are major periods, with French constitutional changes condensed; the brief revolt against French rule in the 1470s is not separately shown.

cities.name: Avignon
cities.note: Avignon passed entirely to Charles II of Naples in 1290 and was bought by Pope Clement VI in 1348. Papal residence began earlier, in 1309. The papal period omits temporary French seizures, including 1663–1664, 1688–1689 and 1768–1769.

cities.name: Aachen

periods.label: France
periods.detail: French occupation, then French Republic and Empire

periods.label: Allied occupation
periods.detail: Allied occupation: American, then British zone

cities.note: Aachen became an imperial city in 1166. The 1794 occupation became formal French annexation in 1801. French rule ended in 1814; Prussian incorporation followed in 1815. Belgian occupation after World War I is condensed into the Weimar period. American forces took the city in October 1944.

cities.name: Cologne

periods.label: France
periods.detail: French occupation, then French Republic and Empire

periods.label: Allied occupation
periods.detail: Allied occupation: American, then British zone

cities.note: Cologne had already gained practical independence from its archbishop in 1288; imperial-city status was formally confirmed in 1475. It was distinct from the neighbouring ecclesiastical electorate. British occupation in 1918–1926 is an overlay on the Weimar period.

sources.title: Cologne museums: Cologne in the Second World War
German Federal Agency for Civic Education: Cologne history

cities.name: Trier

periods.label: France
periods.detail: French occupation, then French Republic and Empire

periods.label: Allied occupation
periods.detail: Allied occupation: American, then French zone

cities.note: This excerpt starts with the renewed acknowledgement of archiepiscopal authority in 1309, not the founding of Trier. Earlier Roman and Frankish eras, temporary early-modern occupations, and the Allied Rhineland occupation after World War I are omitted.

cities.name: Gdańsk

periods.label: Poland (local autonomy)
periods.detail: Polish Crown; extensive municipal autonomy

periods.label: Free city (French protection)
periods.detail: Free city under Napoleonic French protection

periods.label: Russian / Prussian occupation
periods.detail: Russian and Prussian military control

periods.label: Free city (League of Nations)
periods.detail: Free city under League of Nations protection

cities.note: Gdańsk’s Polish allegiance dates from 1454 and was confirmed by treaty in 1466; a short Polish takeover in 1410–1411 is omitted. The 1920–1939 Free City had its own government, with Poland managing much of its external affairs. Soviet capture and transfer to Polish administration both occurred in 1945.

cities.name: Wrocław

periods.label: Hungarian Crown
periods.detail: Matthias Corvinus, King of Hungary and claimant to Bohemia

cities.note: Wrocław passed to the Bohemian Crown after its Piast duke died in 1335. Habsburg Silesia was ceded to Prussia in 1742. Brief wartime occupations, including Napoleonic occupation, are omitted. Soviet capture and Polish administration followed in 1945.

cities.name: Szczecin

periods.label: Sweden
periods.detail: Swedish control; later Swedish Pomerania

cities.note: The Swedish military takeover in 1630 preceded the 1648 settlement. This abridgement omits the Brandenburg occupation of 1677–1679 and Prussian military occupation from 1713 before formal cession in 1720. Soviet capture and transfer to Poland both occurred in 1945.

cities.name: Kaliningrad

periods.label: Duchy of Prussia, under Polish suzerainty
Duchy of Prussia, under Swedish suzerainty

cities.note: The city was called Königsberg until 1946. Earlier Teutonic and Old Prussian history is omitted. Sweden recognised ducal sovereignty in November 1656 and Poland in 1657; the duchy remained in personal union with Brandenburg. Soviet troops captured the city in April 1945; the postwar settlement placed it under Soviet administration.

cities.name: Lviv
cities.note: This excerpt begins after the city’s return to Polish rule in 1387. The West Ukrainian People’s Republic claimed Lviv and held much of it briefly in November 1918 before Polish forces prevailed; that within-year struggle is condensed. The Swedish seizure of 1704 is also omitted.

cities.name: Vilnius

periods.label: Lithuania / Poland / Soviet Russia
periods.detail: Contested: Lithuanian, Polish and Soviet control

periods.label: Central Lithuania (Polish-backed)
periods.detail: Republic of Central Lithuania, backed by Poland

periods.label: Lithuania
periods.detail: Lithuania, following a brief Soviet occupation

cities.note: This excerpt starts at the Third Partition. Vilnius changed hands repeatedly in 1918–1920 and briefly came under Soviet control before transfer to Lithuania in 1939. Lithuanian independence was restored in March 1990; Soviet forces attacked in January 1991 and Moscow recognised independence later that year.

cities.name: Riga

periods.label: Russia
periods.detail: Russian rule; Tsardom, then Empire

periods.label: Contested rule
periods.detail: Latvian independence struggle; rival occupations

cities.note: Riga retained substantial urban autonomy under several rulers. The 1918–1920 row groups independence, Bolshevik control in early 1919 and subsequent German-backed and Latvian control. Restoration was declared in 1990 and completed in August 1991.

cities.name: Tallinn

periods.label: Russia
periods.detail: Russian rule; Tsardom, then Empire

cities.note: Tallinn, historically Reval, was sold by Denmark to the Teutonic Order in 1346. Estonia declared independence in February 1918; German occupation followed until November of that year. Sweden’s 1710 capitulation was confirmed by treaty in 1721.

cities.name: Helsinki
cities.note: Helsinki was founded under Swedish rule in 1550. Finland was formally ceded to Russia in 1809 after occupation in 1808. Independence came in 1917; brief Red control and German intervention during the Finnish Civil War in 1918 are not separate country periods.

sources.title: City of Helsinki: The Great Northern War and the destruction of Helsinki

cities.name: Vyborg

periods.label: Russia
periods.detail: Russian rule; Tsardom, then Empire

periods.label: Finland
periods.detail: Finnish reconquest and administration

cities.note: The Swedish castle was founded in 1293. Vyborg’s capture in 1710 was confirmed by treaty in 1721. Old Finland joined the autonomous grand duchy in 1812. The city was ceded after the Winter War, retaken by Finland in 1941, and captured again by Soviet forces in June 1944.

cities.name: Turku
cities.note: 1229 is Turku’s traditional founding year rather than a precise date of Swedish conquest. The city developed in medieval Swedish Finland. The 1918 Finnish Civil War is not treated as a separate country period.

periods.label: France

cities.note: Luxembourg’s 1697 treaty restoration to Spain was implemented in 1698. The Prussian garrison did not mean Prussian sovereignty; the grand duchy was in personal union with the Dutch king until 1890. French withdrawal in 1814 and the 1815 settlement are condensed.

cities.name: Tunis

periods.label: German / Italian occupation
periods.detail: German and Italian military occupation

cities.note: This selected timeline begins with the definitive Ottoman conquest in 1574. The beys retained substantial autonomy; French protection and Axis occupation were different forms of control.

cities.name: Algiers
cities.note: Ottoman allegiance developed around 1518–1519. The regency later operated with considerable independence. France captured the city in 1830; the timeline groups the changing French regimes together.

sources.title: Algerian Ministry of Foreign Affairs — History of Algeria
Cambridge — A History of Algeria, chapter 1

cities.name: Oran
cities.note: The Spanish withdrawal was agreed in 1791 and implemented in 1792. French troops occupied the city in 1831, a year after the invasion of Algiers.

cities.note: The English cession dates to 1661; the English garrison arrived in 1662. The international convention was signed in 1923, but its administration took effect in 1925. The Moroccan sultan retained formal sovereignty during the international regime.

cities.name: Ceuta
cities.note: The city stayed loyal to the Spanish king when Portugal broke from the Iberian Union in 1640; Portugal formally recognized Spanish sovereignty in 1668. The 1995 change concerns internal autonomy. Morocco disputes Spanish sovereignty.

periods.label: China (special administrative region)
periods.detail: Special administrative region of China

cities.note: The opening date refers to British occupation of Hong Kong Island in 1841, formally ceded in 1842. Kowloon was added in 1860 and the New Territories leased in 1898; today's whole territory did not share a single transfer date.

cities.note: The 1819 agreement established a trading post; sovereignty was ceded in 1824. The island joined the Straits Settlements in 1826, gained internal self-government in 1959, and became independent on 9 August 1965.

cities.name: Malacca

periods.label: British occupation
periods.detail: British occupation during the French wars

periods.label: Federation of Malaya under British rule

cities.note: This selected timeline begins with the Portuguese conquest. The Anglo-Dutch Treaty was signed in 1824 and the final British transfer occurred in 1825. The settlement joined the Straits Settlements in 1826.

cities.name: Colombo
cities.note: The opening date is the establishment of the Portuguese fort, not the conquest of the entire island. The Dutch captured the city in 1656, the British in 1796. Independence came in 1948 and republican status in 1972.

cities.name: Puducherry

periods.label: Indian administration
periods.detail: Indian administration — legal transfer pending

cities.note: The timeline uses actual restorations rather than the earlier treaty dates. British occupation from 1793 continued until 1816 despite the attempted restoration after the Peace of Amiens. De facto transfer to India occurred in 1954; legal transfer followed in 1962.

cities.name: Manila

periods.label: Philippine Commonwealth (US sovereignty)

periods.detail: Restored Philippine Commonwealth (US sovereignty)

cities.note: The British occupation controlled the city and nearby Cavite, not the whole Philippines. The US captured Manila in August 1898. The Japanese occupation began in January 1942; liberation followed in 1945.

cities.name: Jakarta

periods.label: Dutch / French administration
periods.detail: Dutch, then French imperial administration

periods.label: Indonesian / Allied / Dutch control
periods.detail: Contested: Indonesian republic and Allied/Dutch occupation

cities.note: The city developed from the earlier port of Sunda Kelapa. Indonesia declared independence here in 1945, but Allied and Dutch forces reoccupied the city; Dutch recognition of Indonesian sovereignty came in December 1949.

cities.name: Cape Town
cities.note: The timeline begins with the Dutch colonial settlement, not the area's earlier Khoekhoe communities. The Union was initially a British dominion and became sovereign incrementally. South Africa became a republic in 1961; apartheid ended with democratic elections in 1994.

sources.title: South African History Online — English settlement
South African History Online — Cape Town timeline

cities.name: Havana

periods.label: US occupation
periods.detail: United States provisional occupation government

cities.note: The opening date refers to Havana's present site. Spanish administration ended on 1 January 1899. The 1959 revolution changed Cuba's government but did not transfer the city to another sovereign state.

sources.title: Harvard ReVista — Highlights of Cuban colonial history

cities.name: New Orleans

periods.label: Spain
periods.detail: Spain (transitional French administration)

cities.note: Spain received the territory by the 1762 treaty; its first governor arrived in 1766 and a revolt expelled him in 1768. Spanish institutions were established in 1769. France administered the city from 30 November to 20 December 1803 before the US handover. Union troops captured it in 1862.

sources.title: Library of Congress — Louisiana as a Spanish colony
Law Library of Louisiana — Colonial law
National Park Service — Louisiana officially transferred

cities.name: Qingdao

periods.label: German Empire (leased territory)
periods.detail: German occupation in 1897; formal lease from 1898.

periods.label: People’s Republic of China
periods.detail: Communist forces took the city in June; the PRC was proclaimed in October.

cities.note: The selected timeline begins with the Qing government's establishment of a local defence administration. Germany occupied Qingdao in November 1897, before the March 1898 lease. China recovered administration in December 1922. Postwar US naval presence did not replace Chinese sovereignty.

cities.name: Dalian

periods.label: Soviet military control
periods.detail: Local Chinese Communist administration operated under Soviet military authority.

periods.label: PRC (Soviet presence)
periods.detail: People’s Republic of China (Soviet presence)

cities.note: This follows the historic Dalian urban core, not every settlement within today's municipality. Soviet forces arrived in August 1945. Civil administration passed to the PRC in 1950, while Soviet troops remained in the wider port area until 1955; their departure was not the start of Chinese civil rule.

sources.title: Dalian — Russian, Japanese and Soviet periods

cities.name: Harbin
cities.note: The selected timeline starts in 1932. Earlier Russian railway administration was an enclave arrangement, not simple Russian sovereignty over the whole city. Soviet troops entered in August 1945 and withdrew in April 1946; Communist municipal government followed before the PRC was founded in 1949.

sources.title: Harbin — Japanese occupation and postwar history

cities.name: Taipei
cities.note: The timeline starts with the establishment of Taipei Prefecture. Japan acquired Taiwan in 1895; the short-lived Republic of Formosa briefly claimed authority during that year's transition. Republic of China administration began in 1945, and its central government relocated here in 1949. The present row describes administration without resolving competing sovereignty claims over Taiwan.

cities.name: Tainan

periods.label: Republic of Formosa
periods.detail: The resistance government remained here until October 1895.

cities.note: This covers the historic core and Anping. Koxinga's campaign began in 1661, but the Dutch fortress surrendered in February 1662. The Zheng regime surrendered in 1683; formal Qing prefectural administration followed in 1684. The 1895 resistance lasted until October. The present row describes actual administration, without deciding Taiwan's disputed sovereignty.

Same-year rows preserve the Korean War's four changes of control instead of treating the city as continuously South Korean from 1948.

sources.title: US Army Military Government in Korea

cities.name: Busan
cities.note: Japanese forces held the port during the 1592–1598 invasions. Later Japanese trading compounds did not make the whole city Japanese territory. Busan remained under South Korean/UN control during the Korean War and served as a temporary capital. The 1905 protectorate and 1910 annexation are separate transitions.

sources.title: US Army Military Government in Korea

periods.detail: March–August 1945, after the coup against French rule.

periods.detail: Brief control following Japan's surrender.

periods.label: British / French control
periods.detail: British and French military control

periods.label: Cochinchina (French-backed)
periods.detail: French-sponsored Cochinchina government

cities.note: The French captured Saigon in 1859. Japanese troops entered southern Indochina in 1941 while French administrators initially remained. The turbulent 1945 rows distinguish Japan's coup, revolutionary control and the British-assisted French return. The city fell to communist forces in April 1975; formal reunification and renaming followed in 1976.

cities.name: Yangon
cities.note: Alaungpaya captured and renamed the settlement in 1755. The first British occupation ended in 1826; permanent colonial conquest came in 1852. Japanese wartime control ended when Allied forces retook the city in May 1945. The final row groups successive governments of independent Burma/Myanmar, rather than treating each regime change as foreign conquest.

cities.name: George Town
cities.note: The modern town was founded under the East India Company in 1786. After Company rule, it belonged to British India until the Straits Settlements became a separate Crown colony in 1867. The postwar row groups military administration, the Malayan Union and the colonial Federation of Malaya. Malaya became independent in 1957 and joined Malaysia in 1963.

sources.title: George Town, Penang — colonial and modern history

cities.name: Makassar

periods.label: East Indonesia (Dutch sovereignty)
periods.detail: State of East Indonesia (Dutch sovereignty)

cities.note: This follows the Dutch-controlled harbour and urban core after Gowa's defeat, not every neighbouring kingdom. The VOC obtained the port fortress in 1667; Gowa's main fortress fell in 1669. British administration began locally in 1812. Allied troops arrived in 1945, and Dutch civil authority returned during 1946. The eastern federal state joined sovereign federal Indonesia in December 1949, then unitary Indonesia in 1950.

sources.title: Abd Latif — British administration in South Sulawesi, 1812–1816
ANU Press — Anthony Reid on early Macassan history
Indische Kamp Archieven — Celebes occupation and aftermath
State of East Indonesia — formation and dissolution

cities.name: Surabaya

periods.label: Indonesian republican forces
periods.detail: After Japan's surrender and before the November battle.

cities.note: Mataram ceded Surabaya to the VOC in 1743. The Dutch-state row includes the Napoleonic political changes before Britain's 1811 conquest. Indonesian republicans held the city briefly in 1945; British forces captured it in November and handed control back to the Dutch during 1946. Dutch sovereignty ended in December 1949; the federal republic became unitary in August 1950.

sources.title: Howard Dick — Surabaya, City of Work
National Archives of Australia — Indonesian independence

cities.name: Naha
cities.note: Naha was the Ryukyu kingdom's principal port. After Satsuma's 1609 invasion, the kingdom retained its monarchy and Chinese tributary relationship under Japanese overlordship. Japan redesignated it a domain in 1872 and abolished the monarchy in 1879. US administration after the Battle of Okinawa was not annexation; reversion to Japan took effect on 15 May 1972.

sources.title: Japan Ministry of Foreign Affairs — Ryukyu kingdom and Satsuma

cities.name: Dili

periods.label: FRETILIN administration
periods.detail: Following the August civil war; independence declared in November.

cities.note: Dili became the Portuguese colonial capital in 1769. Allied troops occupied neutral Portuguese territory in December 1941, before Japan's February 1942 invasion. Portugal withdrew from the city in August 1975. Indonesia invaded in December and later claimed annexation, which the UN did not recognize. International intervention and UN administration followed in 1999; independence was restored on 20 May 2002.

sources.title: Dili — colonial, occupation and independence history
Western Australian Museum — Battles for Timor

cities.name: New York
cities.note: This selected timeline begins with the Dutch settlement on Manhattan, rather than the earlier Lenape communities. British troops withdrew in June 1775; revolutionary authorities then controlled the city until the British campaign of 1776. British occupation continued until the evacuation in 1783. The 1707 transition reflects the union of England and Scotland.

sources.title: Historical Society of the New York Courts — Dutch rule
Fort Ticonderoga Museum — New York in the Revolution
National Park Service — Battle of Brooklyn

cities.name: Quebec City
cities.note: The city fell to British troops in 1759; France formally ceded Canada in 1763. Confederation in 1867 created a self-governing Dominion within the British Empire, not instant complete independence. Canadian constitutional independence developed later. The earlier English occupation lasted from 1629 to 1632.

sources.title: Parks Canada — Saint-Louis Forts and Châteaux history

cities.name: Montreal
cities.note: This timeline starts with the French mission settlement of 1642. British forces took the city in 1760, before the formal cession of 1763. Continental troops occupied it during the unsuccessful invasion of Canada in 1775–1776. Confederation in 1867 created a Dominion within the British Empire; constitutional independence came gradually.

cities.name: Detroit
cities.note: The timeline follows the French-founded settlement. Britain retained physical possession after the 1783 treaty recognized United States sovereignty, handing it over only in July 1796. British troops and Indigenous allies captured the city in August 1812; the British withdrew in September 1813.

sources.title: Detroit Historical Society — Timeline of Detroit

cities.name: St. Louis
cities.note: Founded by French colonists in 1764 after the treaty ceding Louisiana to Spain, St. Louis initially retained French administration. Spanish officials took over locally in 1770. Although Spain retroceded Louisiana to France in 1800 and France sold it in 1803, Spanish administration lasted until March 1804. The French flag flew during the ceremonial handover on March 9–10, 1804, immediately before the United States took possession.

sources.title: National Park Service — U.S. Takes Possession of Louisiana

cities.name: Mobile
cities.note: The original French settlement was upstream and moved to the present site in 1711. Spanish forces captured the British fort in 1780. United States forces took actual possession in April 1813. The city remained under Confederate control after the 1864 naval battle in its bay and surrendered only on April 12, 1865.

sources.title: Encyclopedia of Alabama — Battle of Spanish Fort

cities.name: Pensacola
cities.note: This begins with the permanent Spanish settlement of 1698 and follows the settlement around the bay as its location changed. French control in 1719–1722 included brief fighting and recaptures. Spain recovered the city in 1781, before the 1783 peace. Jackson occupied it briefly in 1814 and again in 1818–1819; the lasting United States transfer occurred in 1821, not when the treaty was signed in 1819. Confederates held the town until May 1862, while Fort Pickens remained in Union hands.

sources.title: Museum of Florida History — Forts of Pensacola
National Park Service — Fort San Carlos de Barrancas nomination
History of Pensacola — Civil War and colonial periods

cities.name: Baton Rouge
cities.note: This selected timeline begins with the 1763 British takeover of a formerly French colonial area. Rebels captured the Spanish fort in September 1810; the United States annexed the short-lived republic later that year. Union forces first occupied Baton Rouge in May 1862, withdrew on August 21, and returned on December 17. The two 1862 handovers are within the same calendar year.

sources.title: City of Baton Rouge — A Brief History
U.S. Army Corps of Engineers — Baton Rouge history

cities.name: San Antonio
cities.note: The selected timeline begins with the Spanish mission and presidio of 1718. It condenses brief rebel control during the Mexican independence struggle. Texian forces captured the city in December 1835; Mexico recaptured it during the Alamo campaign and withdrew after San Jacinto in 1836. Mexican forces also briefly seized the city twice in 1842, within the Republic of Texas period shown here. Federal facilities were seized in 1861, and United States rule was restored in 1865.

sources.title: Texas State Historical Association — San Antonio
Texas State Historical Association — Bexar County

cities.name: Santa Fe
cities.note: The Spanish colonial capital was established around 1610 on an older Indigenous landscape. Pueblo forces expelled the Spanish in 1680. Vargas received submissions in 1692 but lasting Spanish reoccupation required the violent recapture of Santa Fe in December 1693. United States troops entered in 1846, before the 1848 treaty. Confederate occupation lasted only part of 1862.

sources.title: University of Arizona Press — Beleaguered New Mexico
National Park Service — Civil War along El Camino Real

cities.name: Veracruz
cities.note: This selected timeline starts with the United States siege and occupation in 1847–1848, rather than the earlier Spanish colonial history. Spanish troops occupied the port in December 1861; British and French troops followed in early 1862. Spain and Britain withdrew, while the French intervention supported the Second Mexican Empire. French troops departed in 1867 and republican rule returned that year. The later United States occupation ran from April 21 to November 23, 1914.

sources.title: Library of Congress — Occupation of Vera Cruz

cities.name: Santo Domingo
cities.note: This selected timeline begins when Toussaint Louverture took effective control in 1801 under nominal French sovereignty, six years after Spain’s formal cession. French expeditionary control followed in 1802 and Spanish rule returned in 1809. The brief independent state of 1821–1822 was called Spanish Haiti. The 1965–1966 United States/OAS intervention occurred amid divided control during a civil war and is noted here rather than presented as an unqualified transfer of the whole city.

sources.title: Spanish Ministry of Culture — Santo Domingo independence history

cities.name: San Juan
cities.note: The settlement moved to its present island site in 1521. English forces captured the city and El Morro in 1598 but withdrew within the year. Dutch forces occupied and burned the town in 1625, while El Morro remained Spanish; the town-only occupation is marked separately. Puerto Rico passed to United States control in 1898. Commonwealth status in 1952 did not make it an independent sovereign state.

sources.title: National Park Service — San Juan Throughout Time
National Park Service — San Juan National Historic Site
National Historic Register — San Juan historic site documentation

cities.name: Paramaribo
cities.note: This selected timeline starts with English colonization in 1651, after earlier trading posts. Dutch forces captured the colony in February 1667; the English retook it later that year, and it was handed back in 1668. The long Dutch period includes the Batavian political changes of 1795. Britain returned the colony in 1816 following the 1814 agreement. Internal autonomy in 1954 preceded full independence on November 25, 1975. The brief French raid of 1712 is not treated as a lasting sovereign transfer.

cities.name: Recife

periods.label: United Kingdom of Portugal and Brazil
United Kingdom of Portugal and Brazil

cities.note: This selected timeline begins with the Dutch capture of the previously Portuguese settlement in 1630. The Dutch West India Company administered the colony until the Portuguese reconquest of 1654. The United Kingdom’s full name also included the Algarves. The republican revolt of 1817 controlled the city from March to May. The imperial period condenses the short-lived Confederation of the Equator revolt in 1824. Brazil became a republic in 1889.

cities.name: Panaji

periods.label: Bijapur Sultanate
periods.detail: Selected history begins around the construction of an Adil Shahi palace.

periods.label: Portugal
periods.detail: Portuguese colonial administration; British troops were stationed in the territory during the Napoleonic wars.

cities.note: The opening date is a selected historical starting point, not the beginning of Bijapur rule. Panaji's palace was stormed in 1510. The settlement became the formal Portuguese capital in 1843; Indian forces took control in December 1961.

sources.title: Government of Goa — Adil Shah's Palace

cities.name: Kochi

periods.label: Portugal
periods.detail: Fortified colonial enclave established with the local raja's permission.

cities.note: This timeline follows Fort Kochi, the historic colonial enclave. Other parts of today's larger city belonged to the neighbouring princely kingdom, so their administrations were not identical.

sources.title: UNESCO — Historic urban landscapes in Kochi

cities.name: Chennai

periods.label: British East India Company
periods.detail: A coastal land grant established the English settlement under local overlordship.

periods.label: France
periods.detail: Military occupation of the settlement.

cities.note: The selected timeline follows the English settlement and Fort St George, not every locality inside today's expanded city. The French captured it in 1746 and returned it in August 1749 after the 1748 treaty.

sources.title: Greater Chennai Corporation — Origin and growth

cities.name: Mumbai
cities.note: The 1661 marriage treaty promised the island to the English Crown, but the actual transfer took place in February 1665. This timeline follows the historical island settlement; surrounding districts entered British control at other dates.

sources.title: Census of India — Mumbai district handbook, historical section

cities.name: Kolkata

periods.label: East India Company / Mughal suzerainty
periods.detail: Trading settlement under Mughal and Bengali overlordship; land rights were acquired in 1698.

periods.label: British East India Company
periods.detail: Recaptured in 1757; the Company's wider governing authority developed in stages.

cities.note: 1690 marks the English trading settlement, not the founding of all the older villages that became Kolkata. Siraj-ud-Daulah captured the settlement in 1756; Company forces recaptured it in January 1757.

cities.name: Chandannagar

periods.label: Britain
periods.detail: Selected timeline begins with the Revolutionary Wars occupation; some summaries date this takeover to 1794.

periods.label: India
periods.detail: Administrative control transferred in 1950; legal cession took effect in 1952.

cities.note: Earlier French and British periods are omitted from this selected timeline. The cession treaty was signed in 1951 and took legal effect on 9 June 1952. Integration into West Bengal followed in 1954.

cities.name: Karachi

periods.label: Talpur dynasty
periods.detail: The city was acquired from Kalat in the mid-1790s.

periods.label: British East India Company
periods.detail: Military occupation preceded the annexation of Sindh in 1843.

cities.note: Local histories vary between 1794 and 1795 for the Talpur takeover. British troops occupied Karachi in February 1839, four years before the conquest of the rest of Sindh.

cities.name: Lahore

periods.label: Sikh Empire
periods.detail: Ranjit Singh took the city in 1799 and became maharaja in 1801.

periods.label: Sikh state under British control
periods.detail: A British occupation force and resident supervised the regency.

cities.note: This selected timeline begins with Ranjit Singh's takeover. British troops entered in 1846, but formal annexation followed in March 1849 after the second Anglo-Sikh war.

sources.title: State Bank of Pakistan Museum — Sikh rulers
PIDE — Historical urban development of Lahore

cities.name: Dhaka

periods.label: Bengal nawabs / Mughal suzerainty
periods.detail: Increasingly autonomous government under nominal Mughal sovereignty.

periods.label: British East India Company
periods.detail: Revenue authority was granted in 1765; the old deputy-governor's titular establishment persisted.

cities.note: 1610 marks the city's establishment as a Mughal provincial capital. The East India Company occupied the old fort after acquiring revenue rights in 1765. Pakistani forces surrendered in the city on 16 December 1971.

periods.detail: Federation under British protection.

periods.label: South Yemen
periods.detail: People’s Republic of South Yemen from 1967; renamed the People’s Democratic Republic of Yemen in 1970.

periods.label: Yemen
periods.detail: Sovereignty label: local control has fluctuated during civil wars.

cities.note: The British seized the port in January 1839. This timeline records constitutional affiliation after Yemeni unification, not uninterrupted local government control: the city has seen civil-war fighting, separatist control and renewed internationally recognized government administration.

periods.label: Portugal
periods.detail: Colonial control, interrupted by brief Ottoman attacks and occupation.

periods.detail: Omani rule; civil wars and Persian intervention weakened control after 1718.

periods.label: Afsharid Persia / Omani rivals
periods.detail: Persian garrisons held the forts; the withdrawal and consolidation occurred in stages.

cities.note: The 1740s were a contested transition: sources give different dates for Persian withdrawal and Ahmad bin Said's rise. The approximate interval ends with his consolidation in 1749 rather than claiming a single uncontested transfer. British influence never made the city a British colony.

cities.name: Zanzibar City

periods.label: Independent sultanate
periods.detail: The dynastic separation was confirmed by arbitration in 1861.

periods.label: Revolutionary republic
periods.detail: January to April.

periods.label: Tanzania
periods.detail: An autonomous island government administers non-union matters.

cities.note: This selected timeline begins after Portuguese power was displaced. The sultanate was overthrown in January 1964; union with Tanganyika followed in April. Today's island government retains substantial autonomy within Tanzania.

cities.name: Dakar

periods.label: France
periods.detail: The local colonial authorities joined the Allies in late 1942.

periods.label: Mali Federation
periods.detail: Independent federation from June to August.

cities.note: The selected timeline begins with the French military establishment in 1857. Allied alignment in 1942 did not immediately replace all Vichy-appointed officials. The city briefly served an independent Mali Federation before Senegal withdrew in August 1960.

periods.label: Portugal
periods.detail: Selected timeline begins with the completed Portuguese fortress and associated settlement.

periods.label: Portugal / FRELIMO
periods.detail: Joint transitional government sworn in on 20 September 1974.

cities.note: The timeline follows the colonial urban settlement, not all the surrounding chiefdoms. Earlier Dutch and Austrian trading posts are omitted. A transitional government took office in September 1974, followed by independence on 25 June 1975.
